title: Trump Announces US-Denmark-Greenland Security Deal, Claims 'Permanent Control'
detail: President Trump announced late on September 18, 2026 that the US, Denmark and Greenland had reached a security agreement he called an 'Infinite Life' deal — one he said 'never ends' and grants Washington 'permanent control over security, and all other needs' in Greenland, months after he refused to rule out military force to acquire the Arctic territory. A State Department official said the agreement bars non-NATO adversaries — explicitly naming China and Russia — from building bases, stationing troops or making 'sensitive investments' in Greenland without US approval, and gives Washington the right to build its own military facilities on the island without requiring separate Greenlandic or Denmark approval; officials said the arrangement would remain binding even if Greenland achieves independence from Denmark. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the pact 'permanently guarantees U.S. security interests in the Arctic' and that 'Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America.' Key details — including the scale of any expanded US military presence and whether Washington gains any formal power over Greenland's foreign policy or resource development — were not disclosed; the deal is expected to be formally signed at the UN General Assembly in New York the following week, pending Danish parliamentary approval. The announcement lands two days after NATO Secretary General Rutte's UK visit and the same day NATO's Chiefs of Defence convened in Copenhagen and SACEUR Grynkewich briefed the Pentagon's Colby on Europe force-posture options.

media.caption: Trump says the US-Denmark-Greenland deal gives Washington 'permanent control' over the island's security, September 18, 2026

title: NATO's Grynkewich Briefs Pentagon's Colby on Europe Force-Posture Options
detail: US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, joined a virtual briefing on September 18, 2026 with Pentagon Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby on potential approaches to the six-month review of US troop deployments in Europe. The session is one input into at least four sets of troop-level options due to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth by November 6, ahead of a December completion deadline; Grynkewich did not commit to any reduction of the roughly 80,000 US troops currently stationed in Europe, stressing the review's goal is to push European allies to do more while preserving Washington's ability to meet global commitments elsewhere. The briefing coincided with NATO's Chiefs of Defence — including US Chairman of the Joint Chiefs General Dan Caine — convening separately in Copenhagen for the alliance's September 18-19 Military Committee Conference, where they reviewed Ankara summit follow-up and elected Germany's General Carsten Breuer as the next Military Committee chair, underscoring the alliance's continued shift toward European institutional leadership even as Washington's own posture review remains unresolved.

media.caption: SACEUR Gen. Alexus Grynkewich joined Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby's briefing on Europe force posture options, September 18, 2026
